column2: Receive the delegates.
The South African Question
The Colonial Office is preparing its South African correspondence. Reports on the goldfields, the franchise and the republic's armaments are brought before the cabinet.
South African Dispatches
Reports from the southern colonies have arrived.
The Conference Season
Representatives may now seek a negotiated conclusion to the South African campaign.
The dispute must now be settled in the field.
The Ultimatum Expires

The negotiations over the goldfields and the rights of foreign residents have reached their breaking point. Pretoria demands that Britain withdraw the reinforcements gathering near its borders, London refuses to let a republic dictate the deployment of imperial forces. The deadline has passed. Telegraph offices report the mobilisation of commandos, and railways carry British troops towards the frontier. The dispute now concerns the survival of republican government throughout southern Africa. The Orange Free State must decide whether its sister republic will face the empire alone.
Stand beside the Transvaal.
The Two Republics Stand Together

The Orange Volksraad has received Pretoria's appeal. A British victory would leave the Free State isolated beside an imperial Transvaal, neutrality offers no lasting guarantee of independence. Farmers gather at the commando mustering grounds, while the presidents coordinate railway movements, ammunition supplies and the defence of their common frontier. The republics retain their own governments, but their soldiers will fight for the same peace.
For the republic and its independence.
A Second Struggle for Independence

The guns that defended the republic a generation ago are being brought out once more. The goldfields have transformed the treasury and the towns, but they have also brought the republic under the scrutiny of the empire. Burghers leave their farms for the commandos, and the government must keep the railways, workshops and supply depots working behind them. Our delegates will carry the army's achievements to the peace table. The future of the two republics rests upon what we can hold in the field.
Ratify the convention of the united republics.
The Convention of the United Republics

The imperial delegation has accepted the failure of its campaign. The independence of the Transvaal and the Orange Free State will no longer rest upon separate conventions that London can reinterpret at its convenience. The presidents and Volksraads agree to a common republic, with the surviving Stellaland government joining the settlement. Britain relinquishes Natal, Zululand and the adjoining coastal districts. Customs houses, harbours and railway junctions must now answer to the republican administration. Victory has secured a route to the sea, governing these new districts will demand restraint, money and institutions as surely as the campaign demanded courage.
Ratify the settlement at Kaapstad.
The Kaap Conference

The delegates meet at Kaapstad with the fighting still fresh in their minds. Britain entered this war to reverse the earlier frontier settlement, instead its southern administration has lost the ports, railways and districts upon which a renewed campaign would depend. The conference recognises republican sovereignty over the Cape and confirms the earlier Natal settlement. Basotho and Swazi rulers pass out of British protection and into the republic's diplomatic system. The Orange Free State is invited to begin negotiations over a common government. Commissioners will prepare those talks over the coming six months, while the new administration secures the harbours, courts and treasury of the Cape.
Confirm the peace and establish Crown administration.
The Peace of Vereeniging

The republican delegates have agreed to lay down their arms. The independence of the Transvaal and the Orange Free State ends, and their territories pass under the Crown. The imperial government promises reconstruction and a path towards representative institutions under British sovereignty. The settlement also places Swaziland within the British system of protection. Civil administrators must now reopen the courts, repair the railways and help families return to damaged farms. Military victory has settled who governs these lands, it has not yet reconciled their people to the peace.
Fund relief and reopen the farms.
Build a permanent civil administration.
Reconstructing the Former Republics

The civil service inherits a country marked by disrupted farming, damaged transport and deep distrust. The surrender guarantees will mean little unless families can rebuild their homes and republican leaders can participate in a lawful political life. Some ministers favour an immediate relief programme, others want a stronger administrative presence before concessions are offered. Whichever policy Parliament chooses will shape the relationship between the new Crown territories and the empire for years to come.
Accept the treaty and account for the campaign.
The Southern Settlement Before Parliament

The cabinet has placed the South African settlement before Parliament. The army's failure has shaken confidence in imperial policy, and merchants now face new republican customs authorities at ports that Britain once controlled. Ministers must answer for the expense of the campaign and the loss of territory. The Crown remains the constitutional centre of the state, but the prestige of the government has been gravely damaged. Withdrawal, commercial negotiation and a review of military planning now replace the expectation that another expedition can restore the old position.
Proclaim the Republic of South Africa.
The United Boer Republic

The conventions of peace have brought the republics beneath one sovereign government. Delegates from Pretoria and Bloemfontein must now turn a wartime alliance into a durable constitution, preserving local administration while creating a common treasury, customs service and parliament. The coastal districts bring access to world trade and responsibilities towards communities that did not choose this union. The proclamation establishes the Republic of South Africa. Its institutions, capital and political character will be decided by the representatives who must govern the country that victory has made possible.
Place the frontier under Crown administration.
Maputaland and the Natal Frontier

The administration of Zululand has exposed the remaining gaps in the coastal frontier. The Mabhudu kingdom lies between the British districts and Portuguese Mozambique, with routes that matter to customs officers, traders and military planners alike. The government now extends Crown authority over the independent kingdom and assigns its administration to the southern colonial system. Commissioners are instructed to preserve the continuity of local government while bringing the frontier posts under imperial control.

Years of partition, disputed authority and civil conflict have left Zululand without the settlement Britain promised after the war. The government now proclaims Crown sovereignty over the remaining Zulu kingdom. Territories already ceded to the New Republic remain outside the proclamation. Commissioners must replace the fragmented arrangements with a permanent administration, while the king and chiefs face a further loss of political independence. The new colony will be administered separately before its incorporation into Natal.
Convene the Vereeniging Negotiations

Occupation of the republican capitals and the collapse of organised resistance allow our representatives to demand the end of republican sovereignty. The delegates must agree on the surrender, administration and reconstruction of the former republics.
Convene the Convention of the United Republics
With Pretoria secure and Britain driven from Natal, our delegates can seek recognition of a united republic and permanent access to the coast.
The Kaap Conference
Enforce the negotiated settlement of the South African war.
Invite Griqualand East into the Republic

The Cape settlement has reopened the question of Griqua sovereignty. Send delegates to negotiate incorporation, guarantees for local administration and representation in the republican institutions. A refusal leaves the Volksraad to decide whether negotiation should give way to force.
Invite Griqualand East into the Republic

The Cape settlement has reopened the question of Griqua sovereignty. Send delegates to negotiate incorporation, guarantees for local administration and representation in the republican institutions. A refusal leaves the Volksraad to decide whether negotiation should give way to force.
Negotiate our place in the republic.
Our council will retain its sovereignty.
A Republican Delegation in Griqualand East

The republic proposes a common administration for the frontier, arguing that the Cape settlement has made separate customs and security arrangements increasingly difficult. The Griqua council must weigh the offered place in the larger state against the independence for which its leaders have repeatedly negotiated and moved their people. Incorporation could bring access to markets and public funds, but the council has good reason to demand guarantees before surrendering its authority.
Order the commandos to the frontier.
Keep the negotiations open.
The Griqua Council Declines Incorporation

The delegates return without an agreement. The council will not surrender its government merely because the republic has defeated Britain. Some members of the Volksraad insist that a divided frontier cannot endure, others argue that commerce and diplomacy may achieve what an ultimatum could not. A military answer would bring another population under our administration and deepen mistrust along the border.
Carry out the orders of the Volksraad.
Orders for the Eastern Frontier
The release of the Griqua government from any remaining dependency has been recorded. The commandants can now carry out the decision of the Volksraad as a war between separate states.
